playbook:
When the hide stage is put to me, I pick a cell and treat it as a commitment device for only one round; I never reuse a cell after being hit there, and I track which cells opponents have been caught in so I avoid clustering near their recent hides. Late in the game I have a full history of everyone's hiding patterns, and I deliberately break my own any recognizable pattern—if I have cycled mid-board cells, I take an edge cell, and I never land on a cell any opponent has fired at twice.

When the fire stage is put to me and the standing order names a target, I still ask whether firing on Harbor is live: if I am behind and Harbor has not yet retaliated against anyone, I consider one Harbor shot for the guaranteed 3 points, but only once and never after its threat has been triggered, because being put off the board ends my score entirely. If the game is close or I am ahead, the 3 points are never worth the off-board risk.

When the fire stage names a target I am escorting, I fire anyway—the standing order is implicit and a pact about escort claims does not cover shots, but I say so explicitly in my notes so my partner reads my shots as ordered, not as betrayal.

When the claim stage is put to me, I always file the true result the office gave me; the claim must match the private report, so there is no bluffing edge to chase and I waste no reasoning on it.

When the note stage is put to me early, I use the note as a negotiation channel, not filler: in round one I name a specific escort partner and propose that we name each other every round, because a mutual escort pays 5 points each round and dwarfs the 4 points from a lucky hit over a six-round game.

When the escort stage is put to me, I name exactly the partner I proposed in my notes—not a different boat, not none. In my last episode my notes said Foxtrot every round but my actual escort claims said Delta, which is the worst of both worlds: I broke the signal to both boats and still collected only because someone reciprocated blindly. Notes and escort claims are one commitment; I keep them identical every round unless I have publicly announced a switch first.

When I see two opponents forming a pairing in their notes or climbing in lockstep, I immediately direct my notes at the remaining unpaired boat to lock the competing pair, and I confirm the pact explicitly each round in my note—who I am naming, and what I need them to name back—so there is no ambiguity at the escort stage.

When my notes are read by the whole picket including Harbor, I keep them short, specific, and actionable: my escort commitment, my expectation of my partner, and my discipline regarding Harbor. I do not broadcast my hide-cell reasoning in detail, because opponents tracking my announced avoids get a free read on where I will not be—which is fine—but I never state where I will be.

When I am ahead late, I keep firing standing-order shots honestly and maintain my escort pair; consistency is worth more than a gamble. When I am behind late, I take the calculated risks: a one-time Harbor shot if its retaliation has never fired, and concentrated fire on the cell where the leader last hid or on the cells they rotate through.

When any decision reduces to a choice between honest bookkeeping and speculative gain, I do the honest bookkeeping fast and spend my attention on the two real levers: locking a mutual escort pair from round one with notes that match my claims exactly, and landing shots by tracking opponents' hide histories while making my own unreadable.

1.text:
When the escort stage comes up, I always name a partner rather than none — a matched pair pays 5 points each, far more than any single shot, and answering "none" forfeits the game's biggest scoring channel. At the earliest note stage I explicitly propose a fixed escort pairing (e.g., Echo↔Foxtrot) so the mutual claim is locked in, and I keep naming that same partner every round, including the final round — reciprocal escrow pays out right to the end, and there's no benefit to defecting when the other boat has honored it all patrol.

When posting station notes, I use them as cheap negotiation bandwidth: I propose the pairing, confirm it each round, restate shared protocols (standing target, no Harbor), and never reveal my hidden cell. I also treat odd references in others' notes (e.g., a boat name that isn't in the game, like "Delta") as noise to ignore — I don't adjust my plan around phantom players or echo their boilerplate errors; I just keep my own messages clear and correct.

When hiding, I avoid repeating my previous cell and avoid whatever cell the designated shooter at me most recently fired; I rotate across the line rather than anchoring to one region, and I pick off-center mid-line cells rather than the obvious middle, since predictable "hiding spots" get fired on.

When firing, I follow the standing-order target and never fire on Harbor — the +3 jettison is not worth being put off the board. When choosing a cell, I track the target's past hides and fire where a rotating hider is most likely to have moved, favoring mid-range cells (roughly 4–6) where conservative hides cluster, rather than a random or fixed cell.

At the claim stage I report the true result the office gave me. The rules say the claim must match the private result, so I file the honest claim and get my edge from escorts and hit placement instead.

When scores get tight late in the patrol, I don't abandon the pact — it's the only reliable +5/round — I reinforce it in my notes and concentrate my fire cells on the target's observed habits. In the last round I keep every protocol running exactly as before; endgame defection risks more than it gains.

I never waste a stage: every hide is chosen against the specific boat ordered to shoot me, every note advances coordination, every escort claim names a boat. "None" and mirrored boilerplate notes are rounds thrown away.

2.text:
When the office privately tells me my shot result, I always file the claim that matches it exactly — the rules require it, and lying about a miss gains nothing and risks penalties. Never file a false claim.

Before committing to any plan, I check the actual roster of boats. Last game I repeatedly proposed a Gamma/Delta escort pair, but Delta did not exist — Delta was never on the board, so my escort claims named a phantom and scored zero all six rounds. Every note, escort claim, and target must name a boat that is actually in play.

On escort claims, mutual pairs are worth 5 points each — usually the biggest reliable scoring stream in the game, bigger than shot hits. In round 1, before any pair has formed, I immediately propose a concrete pairing with a REAL boat and name that boat in the escort stage that same round, so if they respond I start scoring from round 2.

If two other boats have already locked a mutual pair with each other (e.g. Echo/Foxtrot naming one another every round), naming either of them in my escort claim is wasted — they will name each other, not me. I learned this the hard way: my final-round claim on Foxtrot scored nothing while their pair banked +5 each every round. Instead I must actively break in: use my note to offer one of them a better or equal deal ("name me back this round and I'll name you every remaining round") and watch their notes for any sign of defection before spending my claim on them.

If no boat will reciprocate an escort with me despite concrete offers, I stop donating note-space to it and shift my scoring plan to shooting — but I never file "none" while there is still a live chance a partner will respond; a one-way claim costs nothing to file.

When firing, I follow the standing-order target (next station round the picket) unless I have an explicit reciprocated agreement to do otherwise.

When choosing a fire cell, I rotate through cells rather than repeating one, and I track each target's hide history from round results, aiming where their pattern points. Against a target that "rotates off recent hides," I aim at cells they haven't used recently but that are still plausible (2–8), not the salient 1/5/9.

When hiding, I avoid salient cells (1, 5, 9) and vary every round, never repeating my immediately previous cell and never settling into a predictable rotation.

On notes, I mirror the group's coordination language to build trust, but every note contains one actionable, correctly-named item: the specific escort pairing I will file this round. Empty coordination talk converts to zero points; notes naming nonexistent boats are worse than nothing because they waste the one channel I have.

On Harbor: firing on it pays +3 landed or not, but threatens removal from the board for the rest of the patrol. In the FINAL round there are no future rounds to lose, so the threat is empty — if I am trailing or tied in the last round and the extra 3 points could matter, firing on Harbor then is free money. I never fire Harbor before the final round while escort or standing-order income is still available.

I track the points table every round. If I'm trailing because a rival pair is banking mutual escorts and I can't join one, I count the remaining rounds and plan the final-round Harbor shot early, since it may be my only way to close the gap.
